# Serendipity, anomaly, and scientific interestingness {#sec-session-08}

**Meeting 8 | Tuesday, October 27, 2026 | 1:00-2:00 PM Pacific**

## Central question

What makes an unexpected observation worth pursuing rather than merely surprising?

## The paper pair

**Pairing type:** First-person marine account / analytical taxonomy.

### Paper A: The Serendipity of Discovery: Life of a Geochemist

@moore2025. **Annual Review of Marine Science (2025).** [Paper / publisher record](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-marine-050823-103645) | [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-marine-050823-103645)

Select two discovery episodes from Moore; track the initial problem, surprise, follow-up, and later interpretation.

*Access: Open-access publisher article; CC BY 4.0.*

### Paper B: Serendipity: Towards a taxonomy and a theory

@yaqub2018. **Research Policy (2018).** [Paper / publisher record](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0048733317301774) | [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.respol.2017.10.007)

Read Yaqub’s taxonomy and concluding implications; the discussant examines the archival basis.

*Access: Open-access publisher article.*

### Why these papers belong together

Moore offers retrospective experience from marine geochemistry. Yaqub distinguishes kinds of serendipity and cautions against assuming it disproves targeted research. An autobiographical success story can illuminate judgment while still being affected by hindsight and selection. [@moore2025; @yaqub2018]

## Prepare before the meeting

Collect several anonymized anomalies from past projects, including artifacts, unresolved observations, and productive surprises.

## Discussion questions

1. Would the observation have been recognizable as consequential before its outcome was known?
2. What distinguishes an artifact from a scientifically productive anomaly?
3. Can targeted research deliberately preserve room for unanticipated questions?

## One-hour meeting

| Time | Activity |
|:--|:--|
| 0-10 min | Independent first judgments; surface disagreements. |
| 10-25 min | Compare the papers: claim, evidence, assumptions, and limits. |
| 25-45 min | Work through the case exercise below. |
| 45-55 min | Translate the discussion into agent requirements and tests. |
| 55-60 min | Record an output and one unresolved disagreement. |

### Case exercise

Blind-sort the cases into debug, pursue, connect to another problem, defer, or ignore. Require a next action and an evidence-based reason. Reveal the eventual histories only after the first judgment.

## Agent-design or evaluation output

Surprise/interestingness rubric: reproducibility, provenance, conflict with expectations, explanatory reach, follow-up cost, and uncertainty. Reward justified redirection, not anomaly magnitude alone.

## Record after the meeting

Record the evidence for your main claim, what changed your mind, what remains unresolved, and one change to the agent or its evaluation. Keep confidential examples in private group notes rather than committing them to this public book.
